utterances.text: Yes. The -- the first thing I learnt was that the MUP really wasn't particularly interested in carrying out ordinary policing activities. They certainly did not behave like any police force I've ever come across before. They were not particularly interested in local crime, traffic control, you know, sort of presence in the streets, doing what we think policemen do. They were mainly in their infantry/military role. So whenever we saw the MUP out in the field, they would be carrying assault rifles, wearing combat kit, combat-type uniforms with some sort of helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps this might be an appropriate time to show you some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Clerk, can the witness be shown Exhibits 17, 18, and 21A and B, and I'll just do all of them at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: While those are being gathered to show you, sir, I believe you mentioned earlier in your evidence that there were different kinds of police, that there were some kind of police wearing normal uniforms and then there was the different kind of police, better equipped, totally different. Would you be able to recognise those uniforms if you were to see them again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, then we'll wait for the exhibits and ask you to look at them. Perhaps we can look at the uniforms first, and I think that's Exhibit 18. Let's display it on the ELMO first of all. Looking at Exhibit 18 - and I'll describe it briefly - there appear to be a series of ten photographs on this sheet, depicting individuals wearing different kinds of uniforms. From your experience as an observer and your military background, sir, are you able to indicate to us whether or not you saw any troops or individuals wearing uniforms of these kinds, and if so, can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: By number.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly saw all these types of uniform being worn in Kosovo. So the first -- number 1 is a typical VJ uniform. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Number 2 is probably also a VJ unit. They're preparing a track change. Three is definitely the type of police force that was used by -- in Kosovo for sort of routine operations and clearing villages and working around Kosovo on Tank Hill, for example, overlooking Lapastica near Podujevo. Number 4, this is something that appeared much later, probably mid-March, and this is a new type of police force which appeared with no real insignia, except it does say "Policija" on the man's arm, but he was not displaying any unit. And also the type of weapon he was carrying would indicate it was some type of special forces of specially trained police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I can just back up to photograph number 3. Is that Cyrillic writing on the shoulder patch of the individuals in number 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Because I speak some Bulgarian, Bulgarian is in Cyrillic so I do read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what does that patch say? Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, "Policija."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's also police, eh? And the weapons, if you're able to tell from the restricted view you have of what they're holding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, number 3, they're an AK47 variant but the Yugoslav-produced variant of the AK47. I think it's called an M70.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 4, this seems to be possibly an AK47 type of weapon with a folding stock, which is usually for parachute type forces or special forces use.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 5.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 5, although this looks like a combat uniform of the VJ, this is again a police unit. These are some of the two types of uniform that appeared on the police arriving much later. So you also see in 6, the same type of helmet is being worn but whereas on the left it appears to be a sort of greeny-olive camouflage kit, on the right they are wearing the typical dark blue of the MUP. In 6 -- well, in fact in both 5 and 6, the soldier in the foreground is holding a sniper rifle. This is another version of the AK47 but a long-barreled weapon, a longer-barreled weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And again there appear to be pocket flashes indicating -- is that again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That's policija again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in number 6, there appears to be a blue uniform with, is that a green kind of a vest or something they're wearing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That's their vest in which they keep their ammunition and bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's typical combat clothing worn by combat troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 7, if you're able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Again, number 7 is something which is a bit more than ordinary police. It's -- they're not army. It's difficult to tell if they're police, but I think, looking at the shoulder flash, it's difficult to make out, but I think this is another special type of police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the weapon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: AK47.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 8.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is -- I can only surmise that this is more of a some sort of paramilitary unit with heavy machine-gun. I can't really tell what type of vehicle it's mounted on, but these units were seen around and they were associated with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 9 is a truck full of VJ soldiers, it looks like. This is typically the webbing they wore. The helmets, I'm now guessing that this -- if this was the VJ, then this would have been taken towards the end of the campaign when the Serbs were leaving Kosovo, judging by their sort of overgrown appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 10 is certainly a KLA fighter. He doesn't have a -- well, the uniform is unusual. This might even be sort of a German or Swiss patterned uniform, with UCK on the shoulder, indicating he is KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And are you able to tell from the very small portion what kind of weapon that might be, if that indeed is a weapon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Looking at the magazine, it appears -- it's an automatic magazine weapon, so again, it would be the back side of an AK47, which was the weapon of choice of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: While we're at photographs, we may as well deal with -- you referred to equipment you saw. Perhaps Exhibit 17, please. Now, Exhibit 17, just so that we're clear, is a multi-page document, but again it has four different pages, each numbered, with some vehicles on it, from 1 to 15. If you can tell us, first of all, if you saw vehicles of this type during your tenure, and if so, if you're able to identify any of them, that would be of a great assistance. Starting perhaps, with number 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I recognise all these vehicles as vehicles that were used in Kosovo. Certainly 1 and 3 came in much later, whereas we saw more of 2 and a great deal of number 4. If you -- I prefer to go backwards from 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sure. Just let us know which one you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is the vehicle we referred to as the Praga, which is actually an anti-aircraft weapon of quite a high calibre, rapid firing, which was used extensively throughout the entire time I was in Kosovo, usually against buildings or positions held by the KLA. It's a direct firing weapon of high velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So it would be used for purposes other than aircraft, at least, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: While I was there, it was regularly used to -- in actions against the KLA and against KLA villages or against Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that's a Praga, then.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: A Praga, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The vehicle above number 2 is called a BTR60, and again this is a vehicle which can move troops and also commandos. These vehicles, I used to see down at Prizren, at the barracks in Prizren, usually used by the army but not exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And if they're used to move troops, would they also be referred to colloquially as "APCs," meaning armed personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It could be. Certainly number 1 is -- is a true APC, although number 2 is a wheeled, if you like, APC, armoured personnel carrier, whereas number 3 is more of an armoured fighting vehicle, which is -- which can be used to deliver troops, but it also has a fairly heavy gun which can actually be used as part of an assault.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you in fact see those vehicles in operation in assault type of situations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Next page, if you would, please, numbers 5 through 8.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 5 is a variant of the T72 which was brought in in March through Mitrovica, referred to as -- its correct designation is M84. And this is a much more powerful, potent weapon than the number 6, which is a T55 type of vehicle, which is very old a 1950s generation tank. Still very effective but nowhere near as fast and manoeuverable or fire control system as good as the M84. And 5 is what raised our sort of hackles, if you like, when we saw these things arriving at Mitrovica, that something was afoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Now, I'll ask perhaps a couple of naive questions, but 5 and 6, you've given them numbers, I take it they're tanks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, they are tanks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from your earlier evidence, you understood that to be VJ or army type equipment and not MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is army equipment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in fact, the individuals riding in the top of number 6 are wearing what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: They are wearing typical tank clothing with the protective head gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. I forgot to ask you earlier: The vehicles 1 through 4, would they be MUP or MUP and VJ or just VJ, or are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: They were certainly driven around by the -- by the MUP, except -- well, both, because, for example, 4, it was usually used in support of the VJ -- of the MUP, and that would actually have a VJ gunner sitting in the back there, firing the gun. Again, 2 could be used by either, whereas 1 and 3 were seen usually sort of by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to pause here to ask a question about what you actually saw. When you saw operations --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- against villages, was it exclusively the MUP or exclusively the VJ or were they together or what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly the normal method of operation was that the -- that the MUP would actually lead the entire operation, and the MUP would provide, if you like, the infantry soldiers on the ground who would actually advance toward the position and take the position. The VJ role initially was to provide heavy fire support. So they would have an outer ring, if you like, of artillery or tanks who could either, beforehand, soften up the target or at any time required could actually shell the target by indirect and direct fire. But all the activity, the sort of going into the villages, clearing the villages that we ever saw, was carried out by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say, "carried out by the MUP, going into the villages," were the VJ present as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The actual assault would be carried out solely by the MUP. Only later would the VJ, the soldiers, the army, move in. Except for one occasion just north of Kosovo -- of Pristina, in the town called Lebane, where a patrol of VJ one day were driving through and a sniper KLA, presumably sniper, fired and wounded one of the soldiers, an officer, in one of the four-wheel drive vehicles. And then the operation, the response, because this was an attack directly against the VJ, the response was purely VJ, and the VJ then assaulted the village. But for the first time, I actually saw a different type of assault. So rather than shelling the village or doing a lot of damage in the village during the assault, they surrounded the village and carried out a meticulous search but without actually any firing taking place. And we went in the village later and there was no sort of wholesale destruction at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because of my non-military background, that I'm not quite sure when the word "shelling" is used, what is shelling? Is that from big -- big guns or does it mean bombs or what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It means all of those. I'm basically -- prior to an assault or if you want to destroy a target by indirect - in other words, without actually soldiers going in and fighting house to house - what you can do is -- I've used aerial bombardment to bomb an area. You can use artillery, which is indirect, which can be from a range of 20, 20-odd kilometres out, you can shell a village from; or if you're using tanks, it has to be direct fire because their range is no more than a few kilometres and they have to fire in a straight line. So -- and also if you use mortar fire, for example, which is also indirect. So to create a great deal of damage, sort of damage to buildings and personnel if there are any open, you would use shelling as opposed to putting infantry into a village and doing house-to-house fighting where the soldiers would obviously have to take house by house, building by building, block by block, making sure that there was nothing left of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the process that you normally saw would be shelling first, then the MUP going in.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And the shelling would be performed by whom; the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: By the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So VJ first, MUP goes in later, and then VJ might come in after that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So it's a coordinated type of activity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, I stopped you describing once. You told us about tanks. Is there anything further you want to say about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, before you go on. Earlier, the Prosecution submitted a list of names of vehicles titled as Recognition Guide for Vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify those names first with the assistance of this witness so we can name the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly. Now, this is not the witness who we propose to call who composed these but he certainly will be able to do that for us. Mr. Coo will eventually give evidence about all of this, but I think -- I don't have that list right here. Perhaps -- do you have the list, the recognition -- perhaps I'll ask a couple more questions, Your Honour, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- while the list is being provided. I didn't bring my copy of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Seven and 8, sir, appear to be like trucks, lorries, I suppose, in Britain.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Number 7 is what's referred to as a Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: A Pinzgauer. And what is that used for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's used for transporting troops, as is number 8, which is another type of vehicle used by the VJ. The Pinzgauer tended to be used by the VJ -- by the MUP, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Pinzgauer was largely by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: By the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in number 8, we see a number of people driving by -- oh, it looks like a crowd there. What kind of uniforms are those we see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Once again, that's the VJ army and it's another type of truck. I cannot give you the exact specification though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I now have that list. Perhaps that list, a copy of that list, can be shown to the witness. And I see because it purports to name these, I should let him tell us first and then ask to describe the terms. I will give you the vehicle list first, the recognition guide.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Have you been given a list? Now, Witness, just before we start, you have not been shown this list before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. You have seen the photographs but you've not seen the recognition guide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I have not seen the recognition guide.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Looking for the first time at the recognition guide, the photograph that you refer to as number 1, you've indicated is sort of an APC; is that correct? That's what you told us earlier in evidence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes. That's the M60 APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And number 2 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Would be the RTR -- I called it the BTR because that's the Russian designation of it, and the NATO designation is BTR60. "VB" indicates it's a command vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Can I just say that although -- recognition and identification are two different skills, and whereas, you know, I'm quite good at the moment on Bulgarian types of weapons, these skills very quickly degrade and although I can recognise what each vehicle is, I don't necessarily -- I can't guarantee that I can actually put, you know, each number to each vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 3, I don't recall what you called it or what you thought it was.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was -- it's -- it's -- I said it was a troop carrier but this one actually had some gun on it so it probably is the M80 APC. Number 4, as I said, is the M53 Praga, as it was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've already described for us what a Praga was.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it's an anti-aircraft weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 5, I think you told us, was a tank.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: M84, which I think I identified correctly, and a T54/55. The difference between the two being the position of the muzzle break, as they call it, where -- you know, where the fat bit on the gun is at the front or at the middle. That differentiates whether it's a 54 or a 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see, so in all other respects, they look very similar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they do, yes. Only train spotters can see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Number 7, you told us was a MUP type of transport carrier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And would you have known what the name of or number designation was or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know. It was Neimar-A [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And number 8? I think you said that you didn't know the type of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But it's a VJ troop transport?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 9. What kind of vehicle is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we call these Bobs. It's a particular Yugoslav vehicle that is not seen anywhere else, it's their own development. So again, it's an armoured personnel carrier, APC, as is number 10, as is number 11. Although number 12 is based on a Russian type of vehicle which in fact the correct designation is BRDM. It's a light-reconnaissance type vehicle. This one is armed with a gun, machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And again, did you see examples of these vehicles in operation in Kosovo during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, we saw -- I saw all of these vehicles in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: 13, 14, 15 appear to be what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: 13 is the -- and 14 are both Land Rovers, and 15 is an American Humvee. The interesting thing is that 13 and 14 were the type of vehicles that the units that -- the MUP units which came later were driving around in. They were not blue or armoured but they were unarmoured, as you see here, painted in a variety of colours. White, we -- we saw this at the very beginning. We saw the Serbs using white vehicles which could be confused for our OSCE vehicles. This is why DZ ordered the vehicles be painted orange. And there was one occasion when some of the Serb vehicles suddenly became orange as well and we protested this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Sir, there is one final photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I have not had an opportunity to give copies to anyone before. I only have a single copy. Might the witness be shown K0215385, and we'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tell us, sir, if you have seen any vehicle of this nature during your tenure. First of all, have you ever been shown this photograph prior to coming to the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. I have not seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you recognise the vehicle depicted in the photograph at all?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you're not able to say, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't hand and heart say that I can recognise -- it's very difficult from the back and from the scale to -- whether there was any foreshortening of the actual vehicle making it look larger than one I would recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The troops, are you able to indicate what type of troops those are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: They are police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: MUP, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Better trained and better equipped than the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think we're going to move on, if we could, to Exhibit -- the uniforms. We've done that. So it's 21 and 21 -- 21A and B, please. Weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish the recognition guide for these? Yes? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all -- I've got a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, could you look at the photographs of certain weapons and tell the Court whether or not you're familiar with these weapons.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite familiar with the four weapons shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And again, just for the record, we have two pages. One starts -- looks like a photograph, and the others look like they're -- well, I'm not sure whether our 20 -- Exhibit 21B is the same as the one that the court document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this is 21A.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: 21A, the one on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What are those photographs of, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, number A1 is an artillery piece which I think is a D30, which is an indirect fire weapon. You can fire at long range, 14, 15, 18 kilometres range, possibly more, depending on the type of ammunition that you use. Used exclusively by the VJ, and we saw this weapon being used in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. You are looking at something that's on the ELMO that I have listed as 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is B, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This is B. Yeah, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, you could be shown the recognition guide. We have some copies here. All right. Just so we're clear, we're now looking at the photograph on the ELMO, and that is Exhibit B1, I believe. That appears to be on wheels, is it, and is it sort of like the kind of gun you'd find on a tank or smaller or larger?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. In fact, according to the recognition guide, I said it was a D30 to D20, which is a slightly different calibre. Again, one of the ways you'll notice is by the thing on the end, called the muzzle break, which I wasn't looking at too carefully but it's 152-millimetre, which is a large round, it's a range of over 20 kilometres. And this is towed behind a truck, on wheels, and then when it's put into position, the wheels come off the ground and the trails here are spread out to give it stability. And again this is a weapon that's used by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you say it has a range of, like, 20 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, at least. Depending on the type of ammunition that you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is an infantry mortar, portable mortar, M70 commander mortar, which is shoulder carried. It's only a small weapon which is -- fires mortars a few kilometres maximum range. And this is the type of weapon that was often see on the -- on the VJ -- on the MUP positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see either one or two in use at any time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 3 is a Scorpion. I think they've got these the wrong way around. The -- the MP5 is number 4. That's a Heckler Koch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So number 4 is actually --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: An MP5, which is a German weapon. They're used by security forces, people like the police, airport police would use this because it's a short weapon. Fire 9-millimetre rounds. And it was used -- we saw this in the possession of the -- of the MUP special forces as the newer, better equipped forces came. Not a weapon we saw with the VJ. And as was number 3 here, which is a weapon called a Scorpion Zastava, which is a weapon produced in Yugoslavia. Also again not used by regular forces but used by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On any of the photographs in this page, did you see any of those in use by KLA forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, they had a variety of mortar, and the odd KLA might have had a three or a four, but only if they'd come into possession by you finding it or from taking it from a MUP or VJ after some action. But these were not weapons that were generally seen. Rarely seen, very rarely seen amongst the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The next page, which I have as A, 21A, do you recognise the five weapons depicted in that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do; all five.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And can you assist us in terms of what they are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, numbers 1, 2, and 3 are basically the same type of weapon based on the Russian Kalashnikov, AK47, which is the typical infantry assault rifle used by both the MUP and the VJ. Number 1 -- the difference between 1 and 2 is that 1 has a folding stock. In other words, it can be shorten. The metal stock that you see can be folded underneath making it a much shorter weapon for fighting in built-up areas, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. The mechanism itself --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Is the same and they fire the same type of ammunition. They're both 762, although there is a version that fires a smaller round and a different designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's not depicted in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you say that number 3 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Is basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- is another variant of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but that was called a Zastava because it's produced locally in -- but it's a machine-gun so it has a much heavier, longer barrel with a bipod and a larger magazine for the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And a tripod, I take it, to steady it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, so -- because it's a longer-range weapon and it has a higher rate of fire, it needs a longer, stronger barrel to withstand the heat and obviously the tripod to stabilise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And who -- did you see that weapon in -- or that type of weapon in use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: By the VJ and the -- and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Number 4 is a sniper rifle. And this is quite a different calibre because its designed for single-shot telescopic rifle, much longer barrel, a better balanced weapon. Called the M76. And again we have seen photographs of the MUP carrying this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So this is -- this is the type of weapon that we've seen in the uniform where they're carrying weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And because this is a Zastava, does that give you any indication as to where it was produced?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it indicates it was produced in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. Number 5, is that the same case in terms of where it's produced?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That's another -- we call it a general purpose machine-gun, GPMG, Zastava M84. The same, except this time, rather than having a magazine, it has a belt-feed but it's an automatic heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Witness. I'm going to turn to a totally different topic now, if I may. Now, reference was made earlier in your evidence to an incident involving Racak, and do you recall being present during negotiations at the Stimlje police station concerning Racak, and if so, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. As part of the ongoing investigations being carried out by Judge Marinkovic into the killings at Racak, we were having regular meetings with the local police commander in Stimlje, and on this particular occasion, we were informed that Judge Marinkovic was going to visit the camp -- the village, sorry, of Racak to carry out further investigations, and she was going to do this with the support and escort of a large number of armed MUP with armoured vehicles, APC-type vehicles, vehicles with heavy machine-guns to provide her with protection. We knew from our discussions with the KLA that if the -- if the Judge came in with this large police presence, armed police presence, they weren't going to take this sitting down, and they would actually sort of -- there would be a confrontation. So General DZ, General Maisonneuve came up with a plan that we would flood the village with a very large number of verifiers with vehicles and good communications, and we also had discussions previously -- Maisonneuve's team had discussions with the KLA to ensure that there were no KLA, armed KLA within the village which would do any harm to Judge Marinkovic, and we had their assurance that nothing would happen to Judge Marinkovic. But to ensure this, we would also surround Judge Marinkovic with our own verifiers, almost like a human shield, to give her the protection she required. Now, we agreed to meet Judge Marinkovic with the local police at Stimlje, and these discussions went on for most of the morning, several, many hours, at which I was present all the time, and the conversation basically hinged about not -- her not going into the village with the police, and the assurance DZ was giving that this would be done. The only condition that kept on being mentioned throughout this conversation - this was mentioned repeatedly - was that if the judge decided at any point to enter the village with armed escort, then we would like at least ten minutes' notice to get our people out because our people are unarmed and in unarmoured vehicles and the last thing we wanted was for verifiers to be killed as well in the cross-fire. And the judge acknowledged this but neither agreed or disagreed. As the conversation went on and was coming to a conclusion, she suddenly announced that ten minutes before, she had already ordered the troops into the village to go into the village and secure the village, at which point I immediately left the room, got on the radio to Maisonneuve, and I just gave him a few words, and I said, this is -- "Maisonneuve, this is CZ. Get out now." And he had ten minutes to get his people out of the village. Well, he had less; he had no time to get out of the village. And it was touch and go whether in fact his verifiers were going to get out in time. And in fact, several verifiers were stuck in the village, and there was a confrontation. We were very lucky not to take casualties. The important thing, I think, in this instance was that DZ, on several occasions, pointed out to Judge Marinkovic was that if anything at all happened to his verifiers and because of her inappropriate anything did happen to them, he would definitely pass her name -- her name would go forward to The Hague, to the International Criminal Court as someone who actually perpetrated a war crime in endangering the lives of verifiers unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence to be that an armed conflict in fact did break out as a result of the MUP troops going in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: She went into the village and there was shooting, and in fact she then withdraw with her people because she wasn't prepared to be there, obviously, in the middle of a gunfight, although she did go in in an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, just before I go to the next topic, I wonder whether the Court -- because this witness has referred to the recognition guides, whether they should be given exhibit numbers. The vehicles then would become 17A --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've got numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Ultimately, sir, in late March the KVM left Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Because we had reached a point where our presence was no longer safe or effective. For example, we were no longer able to access anything worthwhile, and therefore affect any outcomes in Kosovo because we were restricted in moving throughout Kosovo. We were restricted in going anywhere near the border areas into this new enlarged border area. Our verifiers were meeting with repeated hostilities from the -- both the MUP and the VJ. So as I said, we had several instances where our verifiers were severely beaten or threatened, and on numerous occasions our vehicles were shot at and, in some cases, damaged with gunfire. So we couldn't verify. We couldn't move. Our verifiers were in danger of being killed or wounded. Our job basically was over. We could not verify anything at this point, and that was the main purpose of our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So the decision to leave was made and implemented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We had sort of mentioned, I think, previously, a month or so previously that if the situation didn't improve and that this troop concentration, troop additions and so on, if it didn't cease, then obviously we would have to consider leaving because we couldn't carry out our function.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I will return to this general area at the end of your evidence, sir. I want to move on now to another topic. When did the KVM leave, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: About the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The 23rd of March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And by that, you physically left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We formed a very large convoy of all our vehicles and with the support and help of the Serbian Cooperation Commission and the police, we managed to clear Kosovo very quickly and get through the border very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you personally ever return to Kosovo near the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did. I returned on the very first day that the NATO forces Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was the 13th of June?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: 1999. And what -- what did you do upon -- where did you go and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: By this time, I had actually reverted to my NATO role --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: -- as a British army officer based at Rhinedahlen where the ARK is based. I was then put on to General Jackson's staff and was part of his command group together with DZ. And I came into Pristina, and on the second day I was in Pristina I went to the old MUP headquarters where we in fact set up a temporary office, DZ and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And while there, did you see any MUP officers doing -- engaged in doing something?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The -- obviously there was a fair amount of damage in this area because behind the MUP administrative building was the operational building which had taken several direct hits, as did the communications site. And so there was a large amount of damage to the admin building as well. But what we saw on arrival were employees of the building, MUP and civilians employed by the MUP, removing huge quantities of documents and taking them down to trucks and having them shipped out. But the other thing that was very obvious was in a little alcove, an open area by the buildings as part of the building, there was a very large pile of -- there was a large fire burning which looked like rubbish or documents. This was a pile of about the size of a large truck which had been burning for some time and the smoke had permeated the whole building and there were bits of paper flying around. And on the second day I was there, I was tempted to go down and have a look and see what this pile of documents was, and I actually picked up several handfuls to discover -- from different parts of the pile to discover that these were applications for travel, they were ID documents, these were passports, applications for passports. So amongst this huge pile of burning rubble it seemed to be mainly documents to do with personal identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you look at any of the names on any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I looked through the applications and all the names of these people were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I understand, sir, that you actually took photographs of that pile, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you don't have those available?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm afraid that, as I moved from the UK to Bulgaria, a lot of the stuff disappeared into long-term storage and I thought I had taken them out, but I'm afraid I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You say that the size of this pile of documents was about the size of a large truck?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: A truck?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, a large truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It burned for several days. It carried on burning for about a week, this pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, in relation to -- I think you indicated earlier that in Pristina there was the headquarters of Lukic and some people in a stadium, and I told you we'd come back to a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be shown -- is it Exhibit 61 that is -- I believe it is. No. Actually, I'm thinking of the -- no, the -- there's a Kosovo atlas, and I'm afraid I didn't note down the number of that. Madam Clerk? 83?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could be shown Exhibit 38 and turn to pages 19 and 20 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise at pages 19 and 20 a -- which purports to be a map of downtown Pristina, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just so we're clear about a couple of things, perhaps you could tell us, where is the stadium located on this map, if it's depicted at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's this oval location here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And for the record, you're pointing to what appears to be page 19, there's sort of an oval with the number 108 in the middle of it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were the -- you indicated to us I believe that the general headquarters was a building next to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the main administrative MUP headquarters was this building here, 79, 77 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: -- as depicted on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: And right behind it, what is shown as number 77, is in fact a building which is there, which -- I was in Kosovo recently so I know that this is an occupied building, but what is not shown is perpendicular to that building, between that building 77 and the stadium, was the building that was the operational MUP headquarters which was -- had received several direct hits and was -- is now uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And where -- so -- do you know where the office was of General Lukic and -- is it Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Both General Lukic and Mijatovic had offices in this building. They're just behind, perpendicular to 77. And next to that was the communications site, the large tower which allowed them to communicate to Kosovo and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And 108 would be where the helicopters would be landing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the area where you saw the documents burning, is that area visible on this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. It's probably where it says 79 and a little rectangle on 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That you referred to as an alcove.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That would be a sort of outdoor area enclosed by the building there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Now, these -- just wondering, sir, obviously you don't have those photographs of the burning pile available now. If in the course of events, you're able to have access to those photographs, could you forward them to the Tribunal for future reference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, after -- shortly after the KVM withdrawal from Kosovo, did you go to the border crossing with Macedonia referred to as Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that is near, I take it, the Macedonian town of Blace, is it, or Blace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Bllaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Bllaca, sorry. Thank you. When was that? When did you go there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I was there -- after we left Kosovo, I would go back towards the crossing point, especially if -- at this time there was indication that there were refugees already sort of coming across the border around different parts of Djeneral Jankovic, Bllaca, through the minefields and possibly also coming down the road and trying to get through the main crossing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you have any discussion with any of the people that you found at that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Especially on one occasion, and the exact date escapes me, but on the day that for the first time we saw people walking down the railway track, a long what looked like to be a kilometre or two kilometres of people walking down a railway track, wearing coats and carrying suitcases, which reminded me of a scene from the Holocaust, I sort of went down to the field where they were -- they were coming in and I went to talk to the people, find out what had happened to them, you know, how it was that they were actually walking down the railway tracks. They then informed me that somebody -- that the police -- not somebody but the police in Pristina had been going round, telling people to take whatever they could carry, get themselves down to the railway station because they were going on a trip. When they got to the railway station, most of them, because there was some amount of chaos, most of them had their ID cards and ID documents removed from them. This was a story that was recounted to me on many occasions by many different people in this field at Bllaca. And when I asked them why, you know, what was the purpose of, you know, sending you down here without ID documents, they said, "Well, because we were never to return to Kosovo. This was to ensure that there was no evidence of us ever having lived or been citizens of Pristina and Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did they tell you whether they left Pristina voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they did tell me that, why they left, and they left because they were -- they were forced at gunpoint to walk down to the railway station, and by gunpoint they were shoved onto these carriages, not knowing where they were going or why they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And where did they end up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: They ended up for the first three days, the people that came on the train, approximately 20.000, 25.000 people, they were in the field right next to the border, almost in sort of no-man's land. The first day was a nice sunny day, they just sat around. And by the third day, people were dying of disease, cold. By then it began to rain, the field turned into a quagmire, while the others were trying to decide how best to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did the train take them right to the border?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly not, no. It stopped -- according to the -- the -- the stories I've been told by the refugees, as they were, they were dropped several kilometres short of the border and they had to walk along the railway track.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you say you estimate about 25.000.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In what kind of an area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Probably an area of a couple of -- couple of soccer pitches. So people were crammed in. I mean, there was no space between these people at all. I mean, there was -- you could maybe sit down, it was difficult to lie down. There was no water, no sanitation, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: During the early stages of witnessing this event, did you take a photograph of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I took several photographs in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And after you took these photographs, did the numbers increase?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a blown-up photograph under number K021-8722. I don't know whether these have been distributed before.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, you brought a photograph with you to the Tribunal, and we've had it blown up. Is this a good representation of the photograph that you took?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what -- what is depicted in this photograph? Is this the field of refugees or the early part when you first saw it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is still the very early part, because the field hasn't turned into a field of mud and filth. So this is probably within the first 36 hours. This is probably, actually, the end of the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And it's your evidence then that the numbers considerably increased; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. On subsequent photographs, you can't see anything in this picture except black, except bodies, except people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in your estimate, the total number was about 25.000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We think in the first few days about 25.000 people came through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning now, if I may, to the additional summary of evidence, Your Honours. During the course of this discussion, I'm going to ask the Court for permission to move into a very brief private session to ask one or two questions and then move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us earlier about the departure of the KVM from Kosovo, and was there -- and you've told us as well that you met on an almost daily basis with the Serbian Cooperation Committee. Was there some time when you met with that committee where the discussion about the pending departure of the KVM was the topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When, approximately, would you say that those discussions took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: In the -- virtually in the last few weeks, possibly the last few days of our stay in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at one of these regular scheduled meetings, the departure of the KVM was the topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that meeting, did something occur that was particularly noteworthy to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I was given some information which I found rather surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And without disclosing the name of the individual who provided that information, can you tell us the general circumstances about how it was that you had an opportunity to get this additional information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: At the conclusion of one of our meetings, when most of the members who had taken part in this meeting had departed, myself and my interpreter met with this official, and he put a map on the table and began telling us exactly what the future options were for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might we move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. [Private session] (Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber)

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Once we've been assured that your comments can now not be heard by anyone -- are we at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, who was the individual who you met with, in the presence of your interpreter, who spread out a map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that we know who he was, he was the gentleman who had been part of the commission for some time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- he was there right from the very beginning as the -- sort of the main VJ, serving VJ officer on the commission who had in fact disappeared when the new Brankovic commission came in but occasionally put in an appearance again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And he was present at this particular --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He was present at this meeting, and what happened was that it was just himself, my interpreter and myself present when these discussions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how high a level was he with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, he was an extremely experienced officer who had served for more than ten years, possibly as much as 15 years in Kosovo, had a house in Kosovo, had been -- had taken part in the activities in 1998 as a commander in the Djakovica area where various events, fairly serious fighting took place. He was also a commander prior to that in the Mitrovica garrison. And although I can't verify this, by his knowledge, his expertise, his stature, the type of uniforms he wore, he was a -- he tended to wear a special forces uniform but he was very well-informed, very well-respected, and certainly on my trips with him around Kosovo, everybody would sort of defer to him regardless of their rank within Kosovo. So he was known and deferred to. And he was extremely knowledgeable on all matters military in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: His rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He was a colonel, full colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And he appeared to be immediately under whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He worked with the commission with General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's the end of private session. We can move back into open session, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are we?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just waiting for the announcement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you say that a senior official spread a map out; is that correct? And during the course of that, were there discussions about what the plan was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. This official spread this map on the table in front of me, and without any preamble at all, he told me exactly how the plan to deal with the KLA would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, if you are able, I'm going to hand you a copy of a map that has been previously admitted in these proceedings as Exhibit 61. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It's just a map of Kosovo. And I'm going to give you a green marker and ask you if you could perhaps make markings on this in an attempt to outline what it was that you were told and narrate, and then we can have that marked as an exhibit. With the Court's permission, if that can be done. I'm also providing a green marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This is a colour map of the kind produced, Your Honours, of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we have to remember, that by this time, by the time we left, there were already very large numbers of VJ and MUP dispersed in strategic locations around -- around Kosovo. So what I'm going to describe doesn't actually involve a chase. It actually involves a predetermined strategy of eliminating the KLA through a series of geographical points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And I want you to approximate as closely as possible what this senior official told you and what he described to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, he stood in front of me and pointed on the map, a larger scale map, what they were doing, and he said, "Right. Basically we're going to carry on our operations from Vucitrn and push the KLA across towards Glogovac. At Glogovac, there is a large force of --" this was where T72s and T84s were -- "we will then cut off and destroy any stragglers that manage to make it over the hill towards Glogovac." The next part of activity would be that the forces, the Serb forces that were positioned around Podujevo would push Commander Remi's forces over the mountains, down towards Vucitrn where in fact there would be -- since there was a large garrison at Kosovska Mitrovica, they would be cut off and killed, eliminated. So we've gone like this at the moment, so we've cleared this whole area of KLA. They would then move down towards -- by Stimlje and Suva Reka, which was another sort of very large area of KLA. By this time, the -- most of the KLA resistance around Kacanik had already been dealt with. This had been achieved before we left. So this wasn't an important area. The greatest concentrations of KLA were in this part of the country. So through -- via Suva Reka, through the mountain passes, towards Prizren, clearing up all the pockets. Again, Prizren had a very large garrison, reinforced garrison, and they could deal with any sort of pockets around this area. Then moving up towards Djakovica, operations obviously on sort of both sides, taking out any KLA. Orahovac, which was a problem area. Working their way up to Decani, going east -- one part going east to Decani to an area called Jablanica, where one of the most serious commanders of the KLA had his headquarters, Ramush, and eventually ending up in Pec. And therefore completing the operation to eliminate all the -- all the serious hot spots and major groupings of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And that comment was with respect to how they would deal with what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is -- it was purely to do with the elimination, total and permanent elimination, as he put it, of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did he at any point go on to say something else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Again, I found both these events quite extraordinary, that he should tell me this, which is -- although it appears a simplistic plan, a plan like this would actually require a great deal of planning and coordination and staffing. This isn't something you could start tomorrow morning because it seemed like a good idea. This would require weeks, possibly months, of coordinated planning. But the second thing he told me, which -- I remember the exact words. He said to me, "And when we have finished dealing with the KLA, we will remove all the Albanians from the territory of Kosovo forever."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When this senior official told you this, about how this plan was to be carried out, did you understand that to be solely a VJ operation or what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. This was -- none of these operations at this scale could be solely VJ. These had to be coordinated MUP, VJ, special forces, paramilitaries. This had to be a combined action. He also informed me, by the way, that -- at the conclusion of this, when I looked sort of completely puzzled, he said we're only doing a job. We're only saving NATO and you and a job, because if we don't deal with the KLA and the Albanian problem, then you will have to at some time in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have only one question, but before I do that, I wonder whether the map that the witness marked be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 61A.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, in the discussion of the uniforms, I believe you referred to the -- you referred to the word "webbing." Again from my non-military background, I assumed that you meant camouflage pattern, or you may be referring to something totally different. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the camouflage uniform would be just referred to as a combat uniform. The webbing is the sort of harness you wear on your chest which contains ammunition, water, medical supplies, maps, spare ammunition, grenades, this sort of stuff. So it will enable the soldier to carry a lot more equipment on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So, for example, when I asked you about the MUP soldiers wearing a blue camouflage uniform and a green vest, the vest is in fact the webbing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We would call it webbing. You would call it a vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are the questions I have of this witness, Your Honours. Before Mr. Milosevic commences his cross-examination, I wonder whether the Court would consider instructing him to obviously respect the area of closed session. I just want to ensure that he understands the name of the individual is intended to be kept confidential, which is why I asked for private session. If there's some way the Court can control that, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, you've heard that comment by the Prosecution. It is endorsed by the Court. The name is to be kept confidential. Of course you can ask questions about the rest. If you want to ask something about the name, then we should go into closed session to do it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the KVM, you worked on the verification of arms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That was one of my jobs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were all the other jobs you had in addition to this activity related to arms verification? What else were you entrusted with? What other kinds of activity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was not solely the verification of arms. It was the verification of military activities and military personnel within Kosovo. I was also responsible for helping with the training of new verifiers as they came in through our training centre at Brezovica. And of course my major job was to be the liaison officer with the Serbian Cooperation Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned that you were an intelligence officer of the British army.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I never said anything of the sort. I said that -- I think it was pointed out by the Prosecution counsel that I am a military attache. I was one in Poland, and I'm now the defence attache in Bulgaria. I don't see what connection that has with being an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here in paragraph 4 of your statement, it says, "My career in the military has largely revolved around training systems, support, and in the intelligence areas." And you were the British military attache in Poland, that is to say, in line with your profession. Is it your assertion that this job of yours, as you put it, in training systems, support, and intelligence areas, it has nothing to do with intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It depends, Mr. Milosevic, how you define intelligence and intelligence work. As an attache, my job is to -- one of my jobs is to gather information, as is every diplomat's job in an embassy, on the country and to analyse it and to report. It is certainly not my job, if this is what you're insinuating, that I run some sort of network of agents and gather intelligence in some covert way. Everything I do and have done in my work in the military has been a different type of intelligence, and this is often a misunderstanding between what used to be NATO and Warsaw Pact, is that intelligence officers are some sort of counter-intelligence, agent-running officers. This is not anything which I do. Intelligence, in my case, is information gathering, purely and simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely what intelligence officers do. But I did not focus on your duty as military attache but the first part of the sentence, where you say, "around training systems, support, and in the intelligence areas." So the intelligence area is your profession, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It is an area I've been involved in, but my major work has been carried out around training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Awhile ago, you mentioned when you were explaining the range of your activities that you worked on training the newly-arrived verifiers. Since your profession, as you had written it down here as I had quoted it, related to training and intelligence, did you train the verifiers in respect of their intelligence activity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I was training the verifiers in observation and information-gathering activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my understanding, in other words, this is intelligence work. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We were not there as intelligence officers. We were there to carry out our mission as verifiers. The only way to verify anything is to actually go out and observe and gather information. Now, I would not call this intelligence work. This is purely observation and monitoring, something the UN asked us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that your military career has largely revolved around training and the intelligence area, do you consider yourself to be an expert, a specialist in intelligence activity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I would not consider myself to be an expert on intelligence activity as I have spent most of my life being a trainer and, for example, I was responsible for training -- designing the military training of the first armoured division in Germany for two and a half years just before I came to Kosovo; nothing at all to do with any form of intelligence or information gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am just ascertaining what your profession is on the basis of what you've written here, but let's move on to the next question. Are you aware how many members of the KVM came from intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the conditions, the prerequisites for taking people into the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: As far as I understood, what happened was that countries were asked to nominate personnel to attend. In my case, I received a message in Germany, asking if I -- if any lieutenant colonels at the time were willing to go to Kosovo to act as verifiers. I was a serving officer, as I am now, and I was not of any particular conditions that were set on who verifiers should be. All I can tell you is that gathering a force together, quickly, of people who can be sent to a hostile area, a dangerous area to carry out verification without any preparation, without any facilities being in place, can only really be done by, I believe, a military force or an ex-military force because these people are trained to survive in difficult conditions. You could not send pure civilians into those conditions because they would be just unable to cope in the initial stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the criteria according to which the selection of personnel was carried out for the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: What I'm aware of is that each country made a nomination of its personnel with a brief description of their training and experience and qualities, and these descriptions were sent to Vienna, to the OSCE, and the OSCE held boards to actually put the people in the right slots once they got to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My understanding of what you have said just now was that you volunteered to work in the Verification Mission. What were your motives for applying to do this work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think there were several motives. I was appalled about what was happening in Kosovo, and I felt that my sort of experience and knowledge of not necessarily the Balkans but of Eastern Europe, having worked in Poland for several years, there might be some benefit from the language. The Polish I speak might allow me to understand some Serbian. I felt also that my broad career background would actually enable me to work in a mission like this; and I just felt that it was something that I desperately wanted to do, to help just not the people of Kosovo but to take part in this mission which would try and resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of whether the other members of the Verification Mission were volunteers as well, the other members of the Verification Mission, that is to say, your colleagues, the other members?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: All I can tell you with certainty is that I understood that every single person volunteered. There were -- there were far more volunteers than there were people who were actually accepted. So whoever was doing the acceptance and judging the criteria, I cannot say how they did this and how they whittled down the few hundred British names, for example, down to the 115 British personnel who eventually went. So, no, I cannot tell you how they were selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the selection was carried out from the group of names of persons who had volunteered, if my understanding of what you've been saying is correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during his testimony, your superior, General Drewienkiewicz, said that the military personnel of the mission was there -- were there because civilians could not be ordered to become members of the mission, whereas military men could be ordered to do so. So since military persons could be ordered to become members of the mission, they were indeed ordered to become members. How come your boss gave a different explanation, saying that you were ordered to go there, and your explanation is quite different, that you all volunteered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Even if it was different, it's not a matter for this witness. You can comment on it if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
